item.title: Energy Brief: Ukraine's Drone War Cuts Deep Into Russian Refining: Ust-Luga Terminal Hit, Moscow Now Imports Indian Gasoline
item.description:
A Ukrainian drone attack on Russia's top Baltic export port Ust-Luga caps a summer of refinery strikes that have pushed Moscow to import fuel from India and sent diesel exports to multi-year lows — while the US-Iran Hormuz stalemate keeps rerouting global supply.
► Ust-Luga Burning: Ukraine's Refining War Reaches Russia's Export Hub A fire broke out at Ust-Luga, Russia's leading Baltic port for oil, fuel, coal, fertilizer and grain exports, early Friday after an overnight Ukrainian drone attack, Leningrad region governor Alexander Drozdenko said on Telegram. Why it matters: Ukraine has moved beyond targeting refineries to striking Russia's export terminals themselves, directly attacking the revenue pipeline that funds the war — while degrading the domestic fuel supply that sustains the Russian economy.
► Moscow Now Imports Indian Gasoline as Refinery Runs Collapse Russia has begun importing fuels from India, Bloomberg reported, citing Kpler data showing a 42,000-ton cargo of gasoline from Nayara Energy's Vadinar refinery arriving in Russia on August 5. Why it matters: A crude exporter that once supplied India's refiners is now importing finished fuel from a Rosneft-linked Indian plant — a reversal that shows how deeply Ukraine's drone campaign has reshaped global product flows and Russia's place in them.
► Hormuz Stalemate Holds as US West Coast Reaches for Malaysian Fuel Oil With the US-Iran standoff over the Strait of Hormuz unresolved, Brent traded near $87-89 and WTI around $82-84 this week, heading for a roughly 4% weekly gain, OilPrice reports. US commercial crude inventories rose over 17. Why it matters: The Hormuz closure has widened arbitrage windows enough that US West Coast refiners — normally supplied from Mexico and Venezuela — are pulling LSSR fuel oil from Southeast Asia, a concrete measure of how global product flows are being redrawn by the blockade.
► Kazakhstan Accuses Big Oil of $10.7 Billion Corruption at Kashagan Kazakhstan has alleged in a confidential arbitration case that the consortium developing the giant Kashagan oilfield awarded roughly a dozen contracts in the 2000s with unjustified cost increases or through bribery, the International Consortium of In Why it matters: Astana is escalating its fight with the Western and Asian majors that built its flagship offshore project — a signal that resource nationalism is hardening in Central Asia even as the region's crude faces export constraints through Russia and the disrupted Caspian corridor.
► Indonesia Quake Hits Fuel Distribution as Asia's Demand Picture Grows A 7. 7-magnitude earthquake struck eastern Flores Island on Saturday, killing at least 47 people and prompting a 14-day emergency response status through Aug. 28, Anadolu Agency reported. Why it matters: The quake tests Indonesia's fuel logistics resilience at a moment of global product tightness, while India's coal trajectory underscores the disconnect between Western transition timelines and Asian demand growth that IEA and OPEC forecasts are now trying to reconcile.
■ The Bottom Line The defining shift this week is inside Russia: Ukraine's drone campaign has moved from refineries to export terminals, pushing Moscow to import Indian gasoline, crash its diesel exports to multi-year lows, and run refineries 30% below seasonal norms — an exporter now importing finished fuel. Meanwhile the US-Iran Hormuz stalemate grinds on with Brent above $87, visibly rerouting global trade (US West Coast pulling Malaysian fuel oil for the first time since 2023) even as Washington frames cheap American gasoline as its top war goal. Kazakhstan's $160 billion arbitration push against the Kashagan majors and Indonesia's quake-hit fuel network round out a day where supply disruption, not diplomacy, set the tone.

item.title: Energy Brief: Türkiye Pushes Ceyhan as Alternative Oil Hub as Hormuz Diplomacy Pauses; Saudi Oil Sites Hit by Iraqi Militia Drones
item.description:
Ankara is positioning the Mediterranean port of Ceyhan to absorb Gulf crude rerouted around the closed Strait of Hormuz, while a US-Iran diplomatic pause keeps oil prices below $90 and Iranian-backed militias keep striking Saudi oil infrastructure.
► Ceyhan Emerges as the Land Bridge Around Hormuz Türkiye is actively positioning the Mediterranean port of Ceyhan as an alternative outlet for crude that can no longer move through the Strait of Hormuz, according to Anadolu Agency. Why it matters: Ceyhan is becoming the most concrete physical alternative to Hormuz for Gulf and Caspian crude, giving Türkiye and Iraq a strategic hedge against a prolonged closure and reshaping Mediterranean oil trade flows.
► Hormuz Diplomacy Pauses as Oil Slides Below $90 The US-Iran conflict remains in a diplomatic pause, with oil prices plunging about 7% on hopes of a reopening, per today's headlines. Why it matters: The market is pricing a near-term reopening, but the gap between US and Iranian positions on who controls the strait and whether Iran can levy transit fees remains unresolved — leaving prices vulnerable to a sharp reversal if talks collapse.
► Saudi Oil Facilities Under Drone Fire From Iraq Saudi Arabia has been intercepting drones launched from Iraq targeting its oil facilities, with Riyadh blaming Iran-backed Iraqi militias, according to today's headlines. Why it matters: The attacks test whether Saudi Arabia can keep its own export infrastructure secure even as the main US-Iran confrontation pauses, and they keep a risk premium under Gulf oil regardless of Hormuz diplomacy.
► China Acts as the Market's 'Volatility Arbiter' Goldman Sachs analysts Daan Struyven and Lia Thomas cast Beijing as global commodity markets' de facto 'volatility arbiter', per SCMP. Why it matters: China's demand response is quietly doing more to cap oil prices than any OPEC or US policy, while its critical-minerals leverage remains a separate, sharper weapon in the technology supply chain.
► US Shale Holds Steady as Rig Count Creeps Up The US oil rig count rose by 1 to 455 for the week ending Aug. 14, up 43 rigs year-on-year, according to Baker Hughes data reported by Anadolu. Why it matters: US shale is providing a supply backstop but not a surge, meaning the market remains dependent on either a Hormuz reopening or continued demand destruction to balance.
► EU Coal Share Hits Record Low Coal's share of EU electricity production fell to a record low of 9. 2% in 2025, down from more than a third in 1990, according to Eurostat data reported by Anadolu. Hard coal accounted for 3. 7% of gross electricity production and brown coal 5. Why it matters: The EU's coal phase-down is now structural and largely irreversible, which tightens the bloc's reliance on gas, nuclear and renewables at a moment of heightened import-security risk.
■ The Bottom Line The most concrete energy development today is not in the Gulf but on Türkiye's Mediterranean coast: Ceyhan is being built up as a land bridge for crude rerouted around a closed Hormuz, with Iraq already shifting Kirkuk flows through it. Meanwhile the US-Iran diplomatic pause has oil trading below $90 on hopes of a reopening, even as Iranian-backed militias keep striking Saudi oil infrastructure and China's demand response quietly caps prices. The market is betting on a deal; the physical infrastructure is being built as if it may not come.

item.title: Energy Brief: Trump Declares Hormuz 'US Territory' and Threatens Indefinite Blockade; Asian Refiners Pivot to US Crude as Russia Tightens Grip on EU LNG
item.description:
Washington escalated the Hormuz standoff from blockade to territorial claim — Trump says the US will 'keep' the strait and Hegseth vows an indefinite naval blockade plus unprecedented sanctions — while Asian refiners locked in US crude cargoes and Russia solidified its position as the EU's second-largest LNG supplier.
► Trump Claims Hormuz as 'US Territory' as Hegseth Vows Indefinite Blockade The US-Iran standoff over the Strait of Hormuz took a sharp rhetorical and operational escalation this week. Why it matters: A US claim to 'keep' the strait as territory, paired with an indefinite blockade, marks a qualitative shift from a wartime disruption to a permanent US assertion of control over the world's most important oil chokepoint.
► Asian Refiners Lock In US Crude as Hormuz Stays Closed With Middle East crude effectively bottled up, Asian refiners moved decisively toward US barrels this week. Why it matters: The premiums Asian refiners are paying — $8-14 over benchmark — quantify the cost of the Hormuz closure in real cargo terms. This is the market's own rerouting: US crude is becoming the default substitute for Gulf barrels, a shift that, if sustained, permanently reweights global crude trade flows toward the Atlantic basin.
► Russia Solidifies Position as EU's Second-Largest LNG Supplier Despite the EU's phased ban on Russian gas, Russia ranked second only to the US in the value of LNG supplied to the EU in June, with a 24. Why it matters: The EU is still buying record volumes of Russian LNG even as it legislates a ban — a reminder that sanctions and market reality are running on different clocks. Russia is using the window to lock in alternative buyers in Asia, so the 2027 ban may cost Europe its leverage more than it costs Moscow its revenue.
► Russia's Arctic Play: New Ice-Class LNG Carrier Heads Down the Northern Sea Route Russia's second new domestically-built ice-class LNG carrier, the Konstantin Posiet, is heading via the Northern Sea Route, according to LSEG shipping data reported by Reuters. Why it matters: Every new ice-class carrier and Arctic cargo route is a brick in Russia's effort to decouple its energy exports from Western-controlled chokepoints. With Hormuz closed and European routes being sanctioned, the Northern Sea Route is becoming a strategic alternative that ties Russian energy more tightly to Chinese demand.
► Saudi Arabia Launches Red Sea Maritime Defence Alliance; Pakistan Takes Deputy Command Saudi Arabia has formally launched a multinational maritime defence coalition in the Red Sea, with 13 countries joining as members and representatives from 39 countries involved, according to Ilkha and MSN. Why it matters: A Saudi-led maritime alliance with Pakistani deputy command is a concrete security architecture forming in the Red Sea independent of the US. It signals that Gulf states are building their own protection for the one chokepoint that still carries traffic, even as the US focuses its naval power on Hormuz.
► Oil Set for Weekly Gains as Stalled Talks Keep Risk Premium Alive Oil futures were headed for weekly gains of around 5% as stalled talks to reopen Hormuz and persistent Gulf shipping risks kept the geopolitical premium embedded in prices, according to Dow Jones via Morningstar. September WTI closed up 1. Why it matters: The market is now caught between two forces: the supply-risk premium from an indefinite blockade and the demand-destruction drag from the IEA and OPEC forecasts. For now the supply side is winning, but the tension means prices are likely to stay volatile and range-bound until the Hormuz question resolves one way or the other.

item.title: Energy Brief: Shadow Fleet Spill Hits Oman's Coast as UK Seizes Russian Tanker; IEA and OPEC Deepen 2026 Demand Cuts
item.description:
The environmental and legal fallout of the shadow fleet is now materializing on two fronts — a crude spill reaching Omani shores and Britain's first military seizure of a sanctioned tanker — while both OPEC and the IEA sharply downgraded 2026 oil demand.
► Shadow Fleet Spill Hits Oman's Coast; Salvage Draws a Sanctioned Russian Insurer The Caroline Bezengi, a sanctioned tanker carrying an estimated 800,000 barrels of Russian crude, ran aground on June 30 near a marine nature reserve off Oman and has been leaking since. Why it matters: The shadow fleet was built to evade sanctions; it was never built to clean up after itself. A spill from a sanctioned tanker on a sensitive coast forces regulators, insurers and governments into a sanctions-vs-environment trade-off with no clean answer.
► UK Seizes Russian Tanker in English Channel; Putin Threatens 'Response in Kind' The UK has seized the Cameroon-flagged tanker Smyrtos, carrying an estimated $40 million in Russian crude, after Royal Marines and National Crime Agency officers boarded it — Britain's first military seizure of a shadow-fleet vessel (Crypto Briefing; Why it matters: Seizing a sanctioned cargo is one thing; physically boarding and impounding a tanker on the high seas with marines is a step up in the enforcement war. Putin's retaliation threat turns routine shadow-fleet interdiction into a direct naval confrontation risk in the Channel and Baltic.
► IEA and OPEC Both Slash 2026 Demand Outlooks; Fourth Consecutive OPEC Cut Both major forecasters downgraded the 2026 oil demand picture this week. The IEA now expects world oil demand to decline by 1. Why it matters: Two forecasters cutting in tandem signals genuine demand destruction from the Hormuz closure — not just a supply shock. For the first time in this conflict, the demand side is moving the price down against the geopolitical risk premium, a sign the market is pricing a longer, economically damaging standoff.
► UAE Condemns Iran for Attacks on Two ADNOC Vessels in Hormuz Iran attacked two ADNOC-linked vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday evening, the UAE said, calling it 'piracy' and a 'direct threat' to global energy supply. Why it matters: The UAE is now squarely in Iran's crosshairs despite its OPEC exit and attempts to distance itself from the war. Targeting a national champion's tanker fleet repeatedly is a direct economic signal to Abu Dhabi — and reinforces why Gulf producers are accelerating pipeline alternatives to bypass Hormuz.
► ADNOC Unbound: War and OPEC Exit Reshape Abu Dhabi's Strategy Reuters reports ADNOC has become 'more aggressive and nimble' since the Iran war disrupted exports and the UAE's exit from OPEC. Why it matters: ADNOC's post-OPEC, wartime posture is a quiet structural shift in Gulf oil politics — an OPEC founder member's national champion now operates as an independent, aggressive exporter, less bound by cartel discipline and more exposed to Iranian retaliation.
► Europe's Winter Gas Position Tightens European natural gas reserves are back in focus as the region struggles to build stocks ahead of winter, Bloomberg reports. Why it matters: Four years after the 2022 energy crisis, Europe again heads into winter with storage anxiety. With Russian flows curtailed and global LNG competition rising, gas prices are once more a geopolitical barometer rather than a pure market signal.
■ The Bottom Line The shadow fleet's costs are now coming due in plain sight: an 800,000-barrel spill poisoning Oman's coast with a sanctioned Russian insurer behind the cleanup, and Britain boarding and impounding a tanker with marines as Putin threatens to seize Western ships in return. Meanwhile the IEA and OPEC both slashed 2026 demand on the back of the Hormuz closure, pulling oil prices down even as Iran struck two more ADNOC vessels. item.title: Energy Brief: IEA and OPEC Both Slash 2026 Oil Forecasts as Demand Destruction Sets In; Putin Threatens to Seize European Ships
item.description:
The world's two most-watched oil forecasters published sharply bearish monthly reports on Wednesday, with the IEA now projecting the first annual demand decline since the pandemic and a 4.3 mb/d supply drop, while Putin escalated the shadow-fleet war by threatening to seize European vessels in retaliation for EU cargo confiscations.
► IEA Sees First Annual Demand Decline Since Pandemic The International Energy Agency delivered its most bearish monthly report of the war on Wednesday, cutting its 2026 global oil demand forecast to a decline of 1. 6 million barrels per day — a sharp downgrade from the 1. Why it matters: The IEA is now modeling genuine demand destruction — high prices and disrupted supply are destroying consumption, not just rerouting it. That changes the risk calculus: a prolonged Hormuz closure no longer just means higher prices, it means a global supply-demand squeeze that forecasters expect to persist through the year.
► OPEC Cuts Demand Growth for Fourth Straight Month OPEC followed the IEA's bearish lead on Wednesday, lowering its 2026 global oil demand growth forecast to 580,000 barrels per day — the fourth consecutive downward revision, a copy of its monthly report showed, per Reuters. Why it matters: OPEC's fourth straight cut signals the producer bloc itself is bracing for weaker consumption, not just supply disruption. The IEA-OPEC gap on 2026 demand is a live analytical dispute that will shape how markets price the recovery — and how producers calibrate output when the strait eventually reopens.
► Putin Threatens to Seize European Ships Over Shadow-Fleet Crackdown Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday threatened to seize ships belonging to European countries in retaliation for Western moves against Moscow's shadow fleet, calling the confiscation of Russian cargo 'nothing less than piracy and robbery,' Why it matters: This is a direct escalation in the sanctions war: the EU's decision to monetize confiscated Russian oil cargo has moved the fight from financial measures to physical seizure of ships at sea. Putin's threat of reciprocal vessel seizures raises the risk of a tit-for-tat maritime confrontation in European waters, on top of the Hormuz crisis.
► Oil Dips Below $90 as Demand Forecasts Trump Supply Fears Oil prices fell more than $1 on Thursday, with Brent crude dipping below $90, as the bearish IEA and OPEC demand forecasts outweighed supply concerns from the stalled US-Iran talks, Reuters reported from Beijing. Why it matters: The market is starting to price the IEA's demand-destruction thesis over the Hormuz supply premium. If that holds, it suggests the peak-price phase of the war may be passing even while the strait stays closed — a signal that demand, not just supply, is now the binding constraint.
► US, Syria and Israel Agree to Remove Nuclear Material From Covert Site The Trump administration has reached an agreement with Syria and Israel that will allow the IAEA to remove nuclear material from a covert site connected to the former Assad government's nuclear program, according to US and Israeli officials cited by Why it matters: This quietly resolves a proliferation risk that had been a live trigger for Israeli military action in post-Assad Syria. It also signals deepening US engagement with Syria's new government under Ahmed al-Sharaa — a diplomatic opening that has energy and security implications beyond the nuclear file.
► China and India Maneuver Around Russian Oil as US Tariff Threat Looms China's state-owned Sinopec, the world's largest refiner, has been purchasing Far East Russian oil to compensate for reduced Middle East supply, according to the Institute for Energy Research. Why it matters: The Hormuz closure is redrawing the global oil map: China is leaning harder on Russian barrels, and India is caught between discounted Russian supply and a US tariff th...

item.title: Energy Brief: EIA Forecasts 600K BPD Shut-In Through 2027; Houthi Attack Kills Four in Bab el-Mandeb; US Fires on Blockade-Breaking Ship
item.description:

The 600,000 bpd residual shut-in through 2027 means the market faces a persistent supply deficit even after any peace deal — and the agency's track record of premature optimism suggests even this forecast could prove optimistic.
► Houthi Attack in Bab el-Mandeb Kills Four Crew Members A suspected Houthi attack on the Egyptian-owned cargo vessel Tihamah in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait killed four crew members on Tuesday, Yemen's Transport Ministry said — the first confirmed fatalities from attacks on shipping since the Iran war began. Why it matters: The first deaths from Houthi attacks on shipping mark a dangerous escalation. Until now, the Red Sea campaign had disrupted trade and raised costs but caused no confirmed crew fatalities.
► US Navy Strikes Ship Breaking Iran Blockade in Gulf of Oman A US Navy MH-60 helicopter fired two Hellfire missiles at the Panama-flagged cargo ship M/V Vela Nova in the Gulf of Oman on Tuesday, disabling its steering gear after the crew ignored repeated warnings about violating Washington's naval blockade on Why it matters: The US is willing to use lethal force to enforce its blockade — not just interdict but disable vessels. This raises the stakes for any ship operator considering transit near Iranian waters and further chills commercial traffic in the Gulf of Oman, compounding the Hormuz choke.

Why it matters: A force majeure at Zawiya could knock 120,000 bpd of refining and potentially curtail the 300,000 bpd Sharara field. In a market with 5. 5 million bpd already shut-in, every barrel counts — and Libya's instability shows how the Iran war's disruption is cascading into other producer countries dealing with their own conflicts.

With both sides demanding compensation from each other, the gap between a deal and reality is widening, not narrowing.

item.title: Energy Brief: Iran and US Trade Compensation Demands as Hormuz Reopening Stalls; ADNOC Reveals 15 Vessels Hit; Senate Russia Sanctions Bill Targets India
item.description:
Iran-Oman shipping lane talks reach final stages but Tehran insists on seven preconditions including US war reparations, while Trump counters with his own compensation demands. ADNOC says 15 of its vessels have been struck in Hormuz. The Senate-passed Graham Sanctions Act threatens 100% tariffs on Russian oil buyers, putting India directly in the crosshairs.
► Hormuz Impasse: Compensation Demands on Both Sides Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that an agreement with Oman on new shipping lanes through the Strait of Hormuz is in its 'final stages,' but reiterated that the waterway will not reopen until the US meets a set of conditions. Why it matters: The mutual compensation demands have turned Hormuz negotiations into a credibility contest. Iran's conditions package is broad enough to serve as leverage for years, and Trump's counter-demands — including ones rooted in decades-old grievances — suggest neither side sees a quick resolution.
► ADNOC Under Siege: 15 Vessels Struck in Hormuz Abu Dhabi's state oil company ADNOC said that 15 of its vessels have been hit by missile and drone attacks in the Strait of Hormuz since the conflict began, revealing a far wider toll than previously reported. Why it matters: Fifteen vessels hit is a staggering number for a single national oil company and reveals how systematically Iran has targeted UAE shipping. Despite paying Iran billions for safe passage (as Reuters reported in June), ADNOC vessels are still being struck.
► Houthis Hit Jazan Refinery After Makkah Pact Signing Yemen's Houthis attacked Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery on Saturday, two days after Saudi Arabia signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement with Turkey and Pakistan. Why it matters: The Houthis are now directly punishing Saudi Arabia for aligning with Turkey and Pakistan — expanding their targeting logic beyond Israel- and US-linked vessels to any regional actor making security arrangements they oppose.
► ADNOC's $8B Gas Expansion and Hormuz Bypass Strategy ADNOC announced on Monday an $8 billion investment to expand its gas business, including a new domestic gas processing unit at Habshan and a gas export facility at Ruwais. Why it matters: The financial logic of Hormuz bypass projects has shifted from prudent contingency to urgent necessity. Every Gulf state is now investing in alternatives, and the UAE — which already has the most developed bypass infrastructure — is using the crisis to expand market share after quitting Opec.
► Graham Sanctions Bill: 100% Tariffs on Russian Oil Buyers The US Senate passed the 'Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026' on August 7 with a full majority. Why it matters: The Graham Act would be the most aggressive US secondary sanctions regime on energy since the Iran sanctions of the 2010s. India's Russian crude imports have more than doubled since January, making it the bill's primary target.

Why it matters: The scandium loan signals that the US is moving from strategic mineral rhetoric to actual capital deployment — $400 million for a single mine is significant. But with China controlling 100% of scandium processing, the bottleneck isn't mining but midstream.

Neither side is blinking, and oil is climbing back toward $88 on the stalemate. item.title: Energy Brief: Pentagon Pours $560M Into Australian Scandium Project; Houthis Hit Jazan Refinery After Makkah Pact; Vance Calls Modi on Energy and Minerals

The US Department of War commits US$400M to Sunrise Energy Metals' scandium mine in NSW — the largest Western critical minerals investment yet — while Houthi drone strikes on Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery signal that the Makkah defence pact's deterrence is already being tested.

Why it matters: This is the single largest Western government commitment to a scandium project — a mineral vital for aerospace alloys, solid oxide fuel cells, and defence applications where China currently dominates supply. The Pentagon's direct financing marks a shift from rhetoric to capital deployment in the critical minerals race.

item.title: Energy Brief: Iran Sets Seven Demands for Hormuz; ADNOC Vessel Missiled in Strait; Senate Targets Russian Oil Buyers With 100% Tariff Threat
item.description:
Iran laid out sweeping conditions to reopen the Strait of Hormuz — including lifting sanctions and withdrawing US forces — while an Iranian missile struck a UAE-linked tanker transiting the strait. Meanwhile, the US Senate passed a sweeping sanctions bill threatening 100% tariffs on countries buying Russian oil, and Trump announced a $3 billion push on critical minerals to counter China and replenish weapons stockpiles depleted by the Iran war.
► Iran Demands US Concessions to Reopen Hormuz, Missiles ADNOC Tanker Iran's Supreme National Security Council said on Saturday that the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed until the United States 'corrects its behaviour,' issuing seven conditions for reopening the waterway. Why it matters: Iran's maximalist conditions set the floor for any Hormuz deal far above what the US is likely to accept — particularly on troop withdrawal and sanctions relief. The ADNOC missile strike shows Iran is still willing to use force against Gulf states even as it negotiates, which risks pushing the UAE and Saudi Arabia further into the US camp.
► Senate Passes Graham Sanctions Bill, Threatens 100% Tariffs on Russian Oil Buyers The US Senate voted 86-11 on Thursday to pass the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, renamed after Senator Lindsey Graham, who championed the bill before his death on July 11. Why it matters: The Graham Act transforms secondary sanctions on Russian energy into a blunt tariff weapon that could hit India especially hard — a country Washington considers a strategic partner.
► Trump Announces $3 Billion Critical Minerals Push to Counter China President Trump announced a $3 billion government investment in critical minerals and battery projects at a State Department roundtable on Friday, attended by more than 200 mining executives, educators, and investors. Why it matters: The $3 billion package is the largest single US government push on critical minerals and is directly tied to the Iran war's depletion of precision-guided munitions, which require rare earths, scandium, and other controlled materials.
► Aramco's Jazan Refinery Catches Fire; Previously Halted After Houthi Attack A fire broke out early Sunday at Aramco's Jazan refinery in southwestern Saudi Arabia and was later extinguished with no injuries, according to the Saudi Energy Ministry. The cause was not disclosed. Why it matters: The Jazan refinery has been offline for nearly two weeks due to a Houthi attack, and the latest fire — regardless of cause — underscores the cumulative strain on Saudi energy infrastructure from multiple fronts.
► Ukraine Strikes Ilsky and Syzran Refineries as Drone War on Russian Energy Intensifies Ukraine's military struck two Russian oil refineries overnight — the Ilsky refinery in Krasnodar region (processing over 6 million tonnes annually) and the Syzran refinery (8. 5 million tonnes annually). Why it matters: Ukraine's refinery campaign is a sustained effort to degrade Russia's domestic fuel production capacity. The Ilsky and Syzran strikes add to a growing list of Russian refineries hit in recent weeks.

Why it matters: The dual gas and diesel crisis is Europe's most acute energy challenge since 2022.
